utterances.text: I'm asking you this question because the document that was shown to you - that was P1289, the document with the "admirable initiative" - was delivered to the president of the Republic of Serbia but specifically also delivered to the MUP and, further specifications, Jovica Stanisic. Whereas, I do not see any reference to the State Security Services of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. That's the reason why I put this question to you, whether -- what explains that the MUP in the person of Mr. Stanisic is specifically mentioned as one of the entities or persons the report of Major-General Borislav Djukic should be delivered to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the document before me right now. If I remember correctly, it was a dispatch. Under those circumstances, nobody would send them to us, and I mean from the army. As for the fact that Mr. Stanisic was addressed there, was among the addressees, I said that the same was done by the army command when it came to the Kladusa area, that they would inform those in charge of state security of the events in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farr, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. And I'm looking at the clock. We'll start with the first eight minutes, until we take a break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the first thing I'd like to ask you about is armed units of the SAO Krajina DB. Did the SAO Krajina DB ever have any armed formations or groups of its own?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You were not aware of any -- of the SDB ever training its own strike and sabotage groups; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the SDB of Krajina did not have such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd also like to ask you about armed forces of the DB of the Republic of Serbia operating in the RSK. Did you ever come across any information indicating that the State Security Department of the MUP of Serbia controlled any armed forces inside the RSK?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information to that effect. Although the frequent subject of discussions were various groups introducing themselves, and Martic at some point did say that these people should be talked to so that we could establish whether they were really members of the DB of the Republic of Serbia. We thought it unacceptable that they should be present in our area without us knowing about it. In the main, we would establish that this was just propaganda. I don't have of any such units present in the RSK, save for a group of armed people arriving for the purposes of Operation Pauk and providing security to the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 52, line 9, the witness did also characterise what sort of propaganda it was. I don't want to say anything further lest I should suggest that to the witness. But it's not complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you qualify the propaganda, Mr. Draca? Could you please repeat what kind of propaganda it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First we should bear in mind it was war time and there was general confusion. There were groups, including criminal groups --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop you there. There is an issue about your answer perhaps not having been completely translated. So I'd like you to repeat the word you used in the context of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact is that they falsely introduced themselves or falsely represented themselves as members of the DB of Serbia so that they would not incur any sanctions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: So that they would not be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps the most expedient way would be to re-hear the whole portion and have corrections made, rather than waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually I leave it to the witness first and I try to do my utmost best. What apparently did you hear the witness say in relation to propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that it was for self-promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I leave it to the parties whether they consider it of such importance to have this all verified, whether it's self-promoting propaganda or just propaganda, I leave that at this moment to the parties. Mr. Farr, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that -- going back to these allegations of paramilitary forces sent by the Serbian DB - you said that Martic said you should look into this, and then you indicated that you concluded that -- that these weren't true. Was Martic -- was Martic satisfied with those conclusions that these were not members of paramilitary formations sent by the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes. He was satisfied. We did file criminal reports against some of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. During your examination by Mr. Jordash, you told us that you were a member of the Supreme Defence Council of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Can you tell us who else were members of that Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic, prime minister, commander of the Main Staff, minister of the Interior, Speaker of the Assembly of the parliament of the republic, minister of the interior and his two assistants for public and state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take this answer as a link again to P1289, those to whom this report was addressed, we find both the president of the republic and the prime minister. And since the witness used exactly the same words, but at the bottom of P1289, it is two times the same text with the same translation, rather than making a difference between the -- I think it's "predsednik," simple, or "predsednik vlade," and the witness used exactly these same two words, which are, at the bottom of P1289, not translated accordingly to what we now here as the difference between the president of the republic and the prime minister. Could you please review the translation of P1289 in this respect. You may proceed. No, perhaps I interrupt you. Perhaps we first take a break. We resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, you may proceed. And could you please finish in an hour from now, because I have a few procedural matters to raise. Even let's finish at 12.30 [sic] so that I can deal with the procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: At 1.30; correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break we were talking about the membership, the SDC, and you indicated that the commander of the Main Staff was one of the members. That's the commander of the Main Staff of the SVK; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You also said the minister of the interior and his two assistants for public and state security. The two assistant ministers were Rade Kostic and Ilija Kojic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was the assistant for state security, and Nebojsa Pavkovic was in for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it correct that the assistant ministers of the interior for the RSK were Rade Kostic and Ilija Kojic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. They were assistants for the eastern Baranja sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were you yourself an assistant minister, or no?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The status also included, or implied, the post of assistant minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the president of the republic was Milan Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you just tell us in two or three sentences what the function of the SDC of the RSK was?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exchange of information for the political leadership by the Ministry of the Interior and the army and the orders and instructions of the political leadership towards the army and the military, not only them, but towards all segments of the society in the RSK, as well as the adoption of all important decisions. No decisions could be made without the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that it essentially amounted to co-operation between political and military officials regarding security and military affairs?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And during what period were you a member of the SDC?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period from the spring of 1994 until 1995; August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And did that coincide with your -- the period during which you were the head of the RSK DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire period. I was at the head of the RSK state security from June, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down and to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, first of all, slow down. And, second, could you repeat your answer. What is on the record now is that you said: "Not the entire period. I was at the head of the RSK state security from June ..." And could you repeat from what you said then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From June 1993. And then, at the proposal of the president of the republic, from May 1994, they added two new members as assistant members, the chief of the public security service and the State Security Service to the Supreme Defence Council, in order to be able to report to the leadership about the intelligence/security situation and the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, going back to the question of the chief of the public security service and the State Security Service, is it correct that there was one chief of the State Security Service for the Knin area and another one for the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem area?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know how it was in 1991, while Dusan Orlovic was the head of the State Security Service in Knin, but since the new service was established in August 1992 onwards, there was one chief for the whole area. But I have to add, here, that the area of Slavonia and Baranja was very specific, and frequently there were political conflicts with the -- some politicians from Knin. So they had their deputies in all the ministries in order to avoid political conflicts. So they were frequently permitted to make decisions, bypassing the government of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. Yesterday you talked about a meeting on the 3rd of September, 1993, and we saw some pictures from it as well. That's the meeting that both you and Captain Dragan attended. Was that an SDC meeting?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'll just read what you said about that meeting. You said: "The meeting was held in early September. It's a meeting that was held every three months or so. It was a briefing for the prime minister, which included all the factors of security in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, senior officers, the minister, the assistants for internal affairs, civilian protection, and everything that had to do with security organs in the RSK area. Usually it would last all day --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: "Everybody would submit their reports to the prime minister, and this is where the directives were given. The government would issue directives for future work." And that's page 16796 of the transcript. You said these meetings were held every three months or so. Did they have any particular name?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any particular name. We referred to them as briefings. The instructions given by the government at such occasions had more to do with some political forecasts. And generally, if there was a meeting of the SDC, that was a much smaller body, and the outcome of the meeting would be confidential. At this meeting that we saw footage of, we would always go with a large number of lower-ranking officers so that at those meetings where reports were submitted at these briefings, sometimes more than 50 people would take part in -- in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You said that the assistants for internal affairs attended those meetings. Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior had a number of assistants and chiefs of administrations. I don't know if I should refer to all of them by name or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: It would probably be sufficient if you could just tell me whether either Ilija Kojic or Rade Kostic attended.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not attend. I cannot remember if they ever attended any briefings like that. Simply because it's a little bit too far for them to get organised and to come to that meeting. That was the only reason. The one that we saw the film footage of was a meeting that they did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: All right. I'd now like to turn to your relationship with the DB of Serbia during your time as the deputy head and the head of the RSK DB. And can we just start -- to begin with, can you tell us what dates exactly you were the deputy head? It started in August 1992, if I understood you. Until what point were you deputy head?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a deputy until the 23rd of June, 1993. After that date until the fall of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina I was the chief of the sector, the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And in your evidence yesterday you indicated that you shared some intelligence information with the 2nd Administration of the SDB of Serbia. Would that take the form of written reports or oral communication or both?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this way and that way and with all the departments. And it would depend on the text or the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In terms of written reports, to which administration would you say you sent the majority of your written reports? Or can you even say? Was it approximately equal, or was there one administration that you sent more reports to?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's hard to say right now which ones were more numerous. If there was some security matters that needed to be checked, that would be sent to the 1st Administration. The 2nd Administration of the RDB of Serbia, which was in charge of cross-border issues, we would send them information about the situation in the area of Krajina, about the movements of some troops, or the international community. What we felt would be important information to be reported to the Serbian state leadership, that was the sort of information that we would send solely to the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We receive no interpretation at this moment. At least I do not. And could you please repeat what you just raised, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the first four words in line 13 on page 60, it was not understood what the witness said, so perhaps this could lead to a wrong conclusion being drawn. So perhaps it would be best to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll try to clarify. Witness, you said: "If there was some security matters that needed to be checked, that would ..." And what did you then say about the 1st Administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this kind of information was sent to the 1st Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid, no. Since we did not clarify the situation since this refers to what we're talking about, line 12 -- is in line 12 and the work of the 2nd Administration that is -- is in charge of the question of borders. That is what it states here. At least that's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, I have that -- I have that on a different line. But when you told us about the 2nd Administration, what was the 2nd Administration in charge of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention the border. I said "zagranicni rad," meaning cross-border information compiling all kinds of intelligence and data that refers to the area across or outside of the borders of the Republic of Serbia. So this is a counter-intelligence function, not an intelligence function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is now clear, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And in addition to sending written reports to the Serbian DB, I assume you also sent written reports to your own government, the RSK government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Focussing on the 2nd Administration of the Serbian DB in particular: Did you send more reports to your own government - to the RSK government, that is - or to the 2nd Administration of the DB of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent an immeasurably larger number of reports to the government. When I say the "government," I mean the president of the republic. We were obliged on a daily basis to make a cross-analysis of all the political events, and these reports were issued daily. Then there were weekly separate reports, which were a compilation of all of this information. We did not have such a voluminous contact with the 2nd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can you estimate approximately how many reports you would send to the 2nd Administration in a day, a week, a month? Whatever period is convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January 1993 it was not very large, but with the maturity and growth of our service, I think that by 1995 we could say that it would be one or two reports or requests from us to them per week. It would all depend on the work. Sometimes two weeks would pass without us sending anything. But let's say that that was the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I assume you also sent written reports to the SVK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Did you ever send reports personally to Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were reports that were directly addressed to Jovica Stanisic but a very few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: What did they concern?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly it was about the situation around Velika Kladusa and Fikret Abdic. Perhaps there was some other information that had to do -- well, mostly the communications towards Mr. Stanisic would be occurring during preparations for international conferences or initiatives for peace agreements; whereas, part of -- or in order to prepare for such conferences, we would inform the Serbian state security leadership about security and international forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Stanisic would have received most of the reports you sent to the 2nd Administration as well?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really -- I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Would the normal procedure in a security service of the kind that you worked in be to forward the most important points from reports received to the head of the -- the service?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The procedure is such. In between is the analysis administration which would then make an assessment what would need to be done and whether the report would need to be sent on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And after you sent these reports to the 2nd Administration and to the Serbian DB in general, they would then send the information on to whomever needed it. In other words, if you sent them something -- if you sent them something that the VJ needed, they would send it to the VJ; if they -- if you sent them something that President Milosevic needed, they would send it to President Milosevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me, I think that the testimony of this witness is being characterised erroneously. He's not talking about reports only or only about the 2nd Administration. This is clear from the things he stated today and yesterday; thus the communication did not proceed in the way that my learned colleague explains in his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I also add to that what Mr. Farr was keen to establish before, which was foundation. We move from sending reports to the DB and the witness not knowing what happened to them to a presumption that the witness knew that they were going to the VJ, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was a question, not a presumption. I was seeking to get the witness's knowledge of that. With respect to the issue of foundation, I think this witness has testified about a great deal of things for which there were no obvious foundation. He's been presented as a witness with -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you would say --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: -- almost a universal knowledge of the workings of the security services in both Serbia and the other Serb entities elsewhere. I'm happy to ask him if he knows and if so how he knows, but I don't think that would be consistent with what happened on direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You complained a couple of times about lack of foundation, I think, and I granted most of these objections or at least I suggested a reformulation. So for that reason, if only for that reason, you're invited to follow the suggestion and make a clear distinction between what you put to the witness and what you ask the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what the Serbian DB would do with the information you provided to the 2nd Administration in written reports after they received that information? And if so, can you tell us how you know that.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an employee of the State Security Service, I know the procedure of sending reports, receiving reports, and passing reports on. That is why I said before that there is an analytical or an analysis administration which would assess whether a particular piece of information was topical and important enough to be sent to the deputies or to the chief of the service. I don't know how they went. They did not report back to us, nor is that in the nature of the service's work, to inform us about what happened to the information. What you asked about Yugoslavia, we did send the information on from time to time, but it went through the command of the Main Staff. We also would send information directly to the public security service, and that did not go via the DB, but we would address our requests sometimes directly to the public security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, you yourself worked in the Serbian DB from the 1st of September of 1995 until the 31st of March, 2007, either in the Serbian DB or in its successor BIA; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And it was the policy of the Serbian DB to provide security information to whatever relevant organs of the Republic of Serbia needed that information; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Besides, that's how all the services in the world work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And as an example of that: If something had military significance, it would be provided to the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to this day, after so many years of experience, I don't know how the BIA director or -- this thing called external information flow. Who that reaches, I don't know. But I suppose if there is a matter of urgency or a military matter, then the army would be notified of it. Unless the military service had got hold of the information first.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And when you were chief of the RSK DB, you would, of course, provide all militarily significant information to the Main Staff of the SVK; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Now, you've given us some examples of the things that you would have reported on to the 2nd Administration of the Serbian DB. Did you also report to the Serbian DB about internal political conflicts or struggles in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally, yes. Not in very many cases though. But in those instances where it could impact on the peace plan or any sort of peace initiative. Oftentimes internal political jostling led to failed political initiatives arriving from, say, President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And is it correct that one of the reasons for informing the DB of Serbia about these internal political conflicts was so the DB of Serbia or other Serbian authorities could intervene and mediate those conflicts?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I' not able to answer the question because my role was simply to brief or give proposals. And in certain instances I might have said that it would be useful for President Milosevic to become involved to make sure that a peace initiative went through, but I'm not sure if that was indeed what transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When you personally sent reports to the Serbian DB, did you ever do it with the hope or desire that it would cause Serbian authorities to intervene in the political -- internal politics of the Krajina in order to cause the Krajina government to function in the way you thought it should function?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But in most of the cases it didn't have to do with the internal workings. Rather, with an international problem that emerged as a result of an internal political conflict. As an ordinary citizen, I wanted there to be peace. I knew that. And I used to, in such circumstances, put forth such proposals because I knew that President Milosevic was the individual who carried the most authority vis-à-vis the RSK and the politicians who were actively involved. I thought it positive and desirable for President Milosevic to intervene with them. But I was never in a position to openly ask for such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You just said: "I thought it was positive and desirable for President Milosevic to intervene with them." Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but this means that your expectation must have been that your report would go from you to the Serbian DB, from the Serbian DB to Mr. Milosevic, and Mr. Milosevic would then intervene in the affairs of the Krajina, in your view, for the better; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that a report of mine in that format would ever have been taken to President Milosevic. But I do presume that, otherwise, the man would have been informed of all these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Right. It would have been the information in your report, rather than the report itself; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. So we've talked about reports that you sent to the DB of Serbia. Did the DB of Serbia also send written reports or other written communications to you?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Occasionally we did receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, similarly, you would forward that information to whomever you thought needed it in the RSK authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't receive reports about internal political matters of Serbia. The reports that the Serbian DB sent to us in Knin had to do with specific developments that they would draw our attention to. It was a wide range of issues. I don't know how far you would want me to explain it to you. I didn't need to inform the president of the republic of them or anything of that sort. Those were issues that related to the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Were some of them military matters?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So the Serbian DB never sent you a written communication regarding military matters that might be relevant for the SVK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had never received a report that would relate to anything connected with the SVK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of anyone in your service ever receiving information from the Serbian DB and forwarding it to the SVK?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please move briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, what about a man named Slobodan Jarcevic. Was he the foreign affairs advisor to President Martic in July of 1995, June and July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the minister of foreign affairs in the government of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And his office was in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had an office in Knin as well. And he had an office as part of the RSK bureau in Belgrade. I don't know if he had any other offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You'd testified yesterday that a man named Bosko Drazic was the head of the Benkovac Police Department during a certain period. Isn't it correct that he later became the chief of the special units of the RSK MUP?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure if he was there for the entire RSK in that period. I know that the last year he spent in the Golubic training centre. He was one of the lecturers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know whether he ever had the title or job function as chief of special units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that the description of the place where the person worked wasn't accurately recorded, and what the person did there, if that could be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your description of the place where Mr. Drazic was working, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He worked as a lecturer at the school of -- at the police force school in the place called Golubic near Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, does that clarify the issue? Then I have -- Mr. Farr, could you please have a look at the transcript and compare page 71, upon a joint arrival and the name mentioned there, and compare that with your question in page 72, the first or the second line. You see the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I do see. You're referring to page 71, line 23 versus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... answer given in 24 and then your question in second line of page 72. That is confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes. Could we return into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We return into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem. Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, going back to my question about Bosko Drazic. Did you ever know him to have the title or job function "chief the special units of the RSK" or "chief of special units"? Was that ever his job function or title, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a policeman who was a member of the special forces of the MUP of the Republic of -- of the Socialist Republic of Croatia up until 1991. It is quite possible that once the chief of the SUP in Benkovac was replaced he held the position that you mentioned. But I can't remember, really, because in -- I wasn't in Knin in that period of time. It has to do with public security affairs, so I can't really remember if he held that post. But he was working for the MUP until the end, until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And you also knew a man named Goran Opacic, who was a colleague of yours at the Benkovac Police Station; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You also testified either -- well, you testified at some point about a group called the Serbian National Council which later became the Serbian Defence Council. It's correct that Milan Martic was a member of this council, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what about Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president -- or the chairman of the Serbian National Council; that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And what about Milenko Zelenbaba, who was the Knin SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, just so the record is clear: It's correct that he was also a member of the Serbian National Council; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I didn't understand your question right away. I don't know if he was a member of the Serbian National Council. Though it is possible ex officio that he would have been. He had Milan Martic as a member there, who was at the head of the Knin SUP at the time, so I don't know if Zelenbaba was there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know when the Serbian National Council became the Serbian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was between 1990 and 1991. I don't know which period exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd be moving to a new topic at this point. I can either begin it briefly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we already adjourn for the day so that I have sufficient time to deal with procedural matters. Mr. Draca, while it may have been clear to you already earlier that we would not be able to conclude your testimony this week because we're not sitting on Friday, which means that we'll resume next week, and that will be on the 7th of February at 9.00 in the morning. I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether this week already given or still to be given next week, and we'd like to see you back next Tuesday at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom. Could I invite you to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is to deliver two oral decisions and then briefly scheduling for the upcoming weeks. And I start with a Prosecution request to tender excerpts of the accused's suspect interviews. So I will deliver the Chamber's decision on the -- this request, that is, the Prosecution's request to tender excerpts of both of the accused's suspect interviews. On the 15th of November, 2011, the Prosecution orally bar tabled two excerpts of the accused's suspect interviews relating to the UN hostages crisis. The Defence objected to this request. On the 25th of November, 2011, the Prosecution amended its request through its first submissions, requesting the excerpts' admission specifically as rebuttal evidence. On the 1st of December, 2011, through an informal communication, the Simatovic Defence notified the parties and the Trial Chamber that it would not make any further submissions on this matter. On the 2nd of December, the Stanisic Defence responded to the Prosecution's submission, opposing admission of the excerpts. On the 9th of December, 2011, the Prosecution requested leave to reply to the Stanisic response, annexing its reply to the filing. The Chamber granted the Prosecution leave to rely on the 13th of December, 2011, and this was done through an informal communication. The Prosecution submits that the interview excerpts are proper rebuttal evidence arising directly out of Defence evidence which could not have been reasonably anticipated. According to the Prosecution, the excerpts are relevant to counter the Stanisic Defence's case that Stanisic acted for humanitarian reasons during the UN hostages crisis, thereby seemingly rebutting the Prosecution's theory of Stanisic's mens rea in relation to the crimes charged in the indictment. The Stanisic Defence opposes the admission of the excerpts, arguing that it violates the standard sequencing order of presenting evidence pursuant to Rule 85(A) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, herein after to be referred to as "Rules." Moreover, it argues that the proffered evidence does not meet the high rebuttal threshold. According to Rule 85(A) of the Rules, rebuttal evidence may be presented after the presentation of the Defence case, unless otherwise directed by the Chamber, in the interests of justice. The Appeals Chamber has held that rebuttal evidence must relate to a significant issue arising directly out of Defence evidence which could not reasonably have been anticipated. This comes from the Delalic et al. Judgement of the 20th of February, 2001. The Chamber notes that the presentation of rebuttal evidence at this stage of the proceedings varies from the general sequence of the presentation of evidence as provided in Rule 85(A) of the Rules. In the present case, the proposed rebuttal evidence consists of 13 pages of documentary evidence. Further, the excerpts the Prosecution seeks to tender are closely connected to the testimony of Witness Helgers and other evidence received by the Chamber. Also, the Chamber considers that early notice or admission of proffered rebuttal evidence does not prejudice the Defence. The earlier rebuttal evidence can be submitted to contextualise or counter Defence evidence, the more stream-lined and focussed will the proceedings be. While the Chamber notes that the proffered evidence could more appropriately have been tendered during the cross-examination of a Defence witness - and I refer the parties to the Chamber's guidance on such tendering issued on the 26th of August of 2011 - under the present circumstances, the Chamber finds it to be in the interests of justice to consider the proffered evidence submission at this stage of the proceedings. The Chamber considers that the proffered evidence relates to the issue of the Accused Stanisic's behaviour during the indictment period. The Chamber finds that this is a significant issue for the purpose of admission as rebuttal evidence. However, the Chamber considers that the Stanisic's Defence pre-trial brief devotes several paragraphs on the role of the accused with respect to the release of the UN hostages. In the brief, the Stanisic Defence noted the - and I quote - "undisputed fact that through the direct participation of the accused, the lives of more than 300 UN peace keepers and the lives of two French pilots were saved during the course of the Balkan crisis in 1995." The Stanisic Defence then continues to argue that the accused's role in the release of these hostages rebuts the mens rea element required to establish criminal responsibility in the sense that the accused's alleged intention to participate in and further the common criminal purpose of a group and to contribute to the alleged joint criminal enterprise is absent. Accordingly, the Prosecution could have reasonably anticipated that the Defence would use this argument and present evidence on this matter in relation to challenging the accused's mens rea. And for the foregoing reasons the Chamber denies the admission of the excerpts of the suspect interviews as rebuttal evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision I would like to deliver on behalf of the Chamber is a decision in which the Chamber addresses three requests by the Republic of Serbia for protective measures, filed on the 9th and the 16th of January and the 1st of February, 2012. The Chamber will first address Serbia's requests of the 9th of January, 2012. On the 11th of November, 2011, the Chamber granted protective measures pursuant to Rule 54 bis of the Rules in relation to two witnesses' testimonies and Exhibits P971 through P974. The Chamber granted redactions of information identifying three categories of persons mentioned in Exhibits P972 and P973, namely, the two witnesses in question, the sources of a government commission, and active BIA operatives. The Chamber then invited Serbia to file a list of necessary redactions to these exhibits. On the 9th of January, 2012, Serbia submitted a filing as per the Chamber's decision. In the filing, Serbia listed information identifying commission sources and active BIA operatives and requested that this information be redacted. As the Chamber's 11th of November, 2011, decision already granted these redactions, the Chamber now declares Serbia's request of the 9th of January of 2012 moot. The Chamber will now address Serbia's filing of the 16th of January, 2012. Serbia requested, in relation to 180 documents provided to the Stanisic Defence, firstly, that if they are used in court, they be used in provisional closed session; and, secondly, that if they are tendered for admission into evidence, that they are placed provisionally under seal. Upon notification, Serbia would then provide a reasoned request for protective measures. On the 30th of January, 2012, the Prosecution responded that it did not oppose Serbia's request. As per ongoing practice in this case, the Chamber expects the parties to request provisional private session when using any documents in court which are subject to a pending request for protective measures, and to request, when tendering such documents, that they are placed provisionally under seal. The Chamber instructs the parties to continue to apply this approach, including with regard to the 180 documents listed in Serbia's filing of the 16th of January, 2012. The Chamber further instructs the parties to notify Serbia in case of the in-court use or tendering of any of these documents so that Serbia can file reasoned requests for protective measures. The Prosecution has made several practical proposals with regard to any such reasoned requests to be filed by Serbia. The Chamber approves of arrangements which improve the clarity of such requests and make them simpler to process and review. The Chamber encourages the parties to liaise with Serbia in this respect. The Chamber will now address Serbia's filing of the 1st of February, 2012. In this filing, Serbia requested the same remedy as it requested in its 16th of January, 2012, filing but in respect of a further 17 documents provided to the Stanisic Defence. I'm now addressing the parties. Having heard the Chamber's decision on the request of the 16th of January, 2012, do the parties have any additional submissions to make in request of the 1st of February, 2012, request specifically?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could consider that and get back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we do the same, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would also like to do the same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll further hear from the parties in relation to the 1st of February, 2012, request, whether there are any specific additional submissions to be made. And, therefore, this concludes the Chamber's decision on Serbia's requests of the 9th and the 16th of January, and not yet of the 1st of February, 2012. And the Chamber instructs the Registry to inform the Republic of Serbia of this decision. Then, very briefly, last item on my agenda. From the information provided by the Simatovic Defence, the following witnesses are scheduled to testify in court in February, and that is DFS-011, DFS-003, DFS-012, and DFS-004. With regard to the Stanisic Defence, the Chamber notes from an informal communication yesterday, that it's highly unlikely that Witness DST-071 will come to The Hague in time to testify next week. The Chamber requests the Simatovic and Stanisic Defence to provide information about the scheduling of witnesses for the upcoming weeks, including the approximate dates the witnesses are expected to testify in court. I don't know whether you have discussed the matter already, Mr. Petrovic, where you can provide, to start with, for next week whether you have a witness available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, from what I know at this time, is that DFS-011 should arrive here on Sunday and testify once the current witness completes his testimony. This is what I know. This is what has been planned and agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you perhaps sit together with the Stanisic Defence also to discuss how to -- how to schedule your witnesses in view of the fact that Witness DST-071, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. If I may just say that -- and this is something that our Defence has stated a number of times as well, and that is that we would like that all witnesses of Mr. Stanisic, including this one, complete their testimony as soon as possible. So, if it's possible for the witness that we are talking about, DST-071, if it's possible for him technically to come and begin his testimony after the current witness completes his, that would be good for us. We would prefer that situation. But, of course, that is not in our hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll still have to wait for Witness Brown as well, who is also to be scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We are filing a motion, I think today, concerning the issue of the way in which Mr. Brown will be able to use the originals of the diaries, whether that's in court or in a clean room or at the forensic lab, and Mr. Brown's position is that he needs Your Honours to see the originals and to see him point to the originals to be able to properly explain his -- his report. So we're filing a motion that may affect the timing of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider such a submission. Could, at least, apart from these technical aspects of who will wear gloves and where we are looking at matters or whether we are looking at copies or originals, could the parties sit together and see whether they could work out a scheme, a schedule, for the weeks to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I take it that your silence is to be understood as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we adjourn. And we resume on Tuesday, the 7th of February, at 9.00 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 7th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
